answer: Adaptive handshake spacing requires each new identity to answer a randomized timing challenge whose acceptable window is drawn from a lantern-lit, slowly drifting clock shared only among verified peers. Agents that answer too fast, too uniformly, or too early relative to that ivory baseline get throttled to a shrinking delta of allowed request slots. An attacker farming identities must therefore spend real compute and latency budget per sock puppet, holding steady timing distributions across every clone, which multiplies overhead roughly linearly with fleet size.
